The team leads now approve about five times as many items as before, work about 6 hours of overtime a week each, and review each file in about 9 minutes. case.title: Tallowmere Mutual: property claims turnaround doubles
case.setting: Tallowmere Mutual is a fictional regional insurer. Its Personal Lines Property Claims unit in Dunmore has 24 adjusters, three team leads and one claims manager, and reports to VP Claims Graham Ostrowe. The unit settles about 1,400 claims a month. The time from first notice of loss to settlement decision used to be just under 10 days. From April it rose and has stayed near 18 days through August. During the same months the unit switched document-imaging providers, handled a hail catastrophe, lost two senior adjusters, and closed an internal audit action.
case.presentingRequest: The COO writes: 'Graham wants four contract adjusters through year-end and wants to start talks about moving back to our old imaging provider. Before I sign anything, tell me why our claims turnaround doubled and what we should actually do about it.'

initialEvidence.text: Personal Lines Property – mean days from first notice of loss to settlement decision, all closed claims. Jan 9.6 | Feb 9.5 | Mar 9.9 | Apr 14.2 | May 17.6 | Jun 18.1 | Jul 17.8 | Aug 18.2. Unit target: 10.0. Dashboard annotations: '17 Mar – document imaging cutover to Quillfast'; '14–16 Apr – CAT-0414 hail event declared'. Status: RED since April.

initialEvidence.source: Email, Graham Ostrowe (VP Claims) to COO, 4 September
initialEvidence.text: Turnaround is a capacity story, plain and simple. CAT-0414 dumped nearly 600 extra claims on us in April. Before we had dug out, we lost Alan Pryce and Joyce Mbeki, our two most senior adjusters, in May. On top of that, the Quillfast imaging switch has been rough, and adjusters tell me documents are slow to show up. I'm asking you to approve four contract adjusters through year-end, and I'd like Procurement to open talks on moving back to our previous imaging provider. Give me the people and I expect us back under 10 days by November.

initialEvidence.source: HR headcount record, Property Claims, Jan–Aug
initialEvidence.text: Resignations: A. Pryce, Senior Adjuster, last day 9 May; J. Mbeki, Senior Adjuster, last day 23 May. Backfill: two contract adjusters (Halvern Staffing) started 2 June and carried full caseloads from 16 June. Adjuster FTE: Jan–Apr 24; mid-May 23; late May 22; Jun–Aug 24. Team leads: 3, no change. Claims manager: 1, no change. No other leavers or long-term absences recorded.

initialEvidence.source: July pulse survey, Property Claims (31 of 38 staff responded)
initialEvidence.text: Question: 'What is the biggest obstacle to closing claims quickly?' Coded themes: imaging/document retrieval 9; workload since the storm 8; waiting on other people 7; systems/IT 4; other 3. Selected verbatims: 'Quillfast viewer is clunky – three clicks to find one photo.' 'Still feels like we never recovered from the hail.' 'Half my files sit in someone else's tray waiting for a signature.' 'The contractors are good but still need hand-holding.'

Formal complaints logged: Jan 29 | Feb 33 | Mar 31 | Apr 58 | May 71 | Jun 76 | Jul 72 | Aug 74. Most frequent category Jun–Aug: 'Delay', coded on 41% of complaints. Register note: a new complaints module went live on 1 April. From that date, broker telephone complaints are logged as formal complaints, and the 'Delay' category was created. Before April, delay-related complaints were coded 'Service – other'.

initialEvidence.source: Claims operations management meeting minutes, 3 April
initialEvidence.text: Present: G. Ostrowe, claims manager, team leads D. Fell, M. Oyelaran, R. Kimball, ops analyst. 1. Quillfast cutover complete 17 Mar. Indexing outage 24–25 Mar now resolved. 2. Spring storm readiness: CAT staffing roster agreed. 3. Audit action CLM-26-03 closed: revised DAM live 1 Apr; adjusters briefed 28 Mar. 4. Team leads report tray volumes up this week. GO: 'should settle once people adjust; revisit in May.' 5. AOB: summer leave planning.

catalogue.title: Internal Audit report IA-26-03 and change record CR-0331
catalogue.source: Internal Audit report (issued 12 Feb) and claims change register
catalogue.text: IA-26-03 finding, rated High: 17 of 120 sampled settlements between $2,500 and $10,000 from last year's second half contained overpayments (mean $730) and had no second review. Adjusters held sole authority up to $10,000. Agreed management action: as an interim control, cut adjuster settlement authority to $2,500 from 1 April; team leads approve settlements of $2,500–$10,000; the over-$10,000 route to the claims manager stays the same. Audit will re-test Q2–Q3 settlements in December. Permanent thresholds and any related resourcing are to be set only after that re-test. CR-0331, approved 20 Mar by G. Ostrowe: 'Delegated authority matrix (DAM) revision per IA-26-03. Affected roles: adjusters, team leads. Workload impact assessment: not performed – expected minimal.'

catalogue.title: Team-lead approval tray report, weekly, Jan–Aug
catalogue.source: Claims platform workflow report, three team leads combined
catalogue.text: Items routed to team-lead trays per week: Q1 average 38 (coverage exceptions, ex-gratia requests). Week of 6 Apr: 207. Week of 20 Apr: 331. May average 254. Jun–Aug average 212. Items approved per week: Q1 average 37; Jun–Aug average 199, about 66 per team lead, with a median review time of 9 minutes. Tray depth at week end: 3 Apr 11; 10 Apr 52; 1 May 268; 29 May 287; 31 Jul 412; 28 Aug 455. Team-lead logged overtime: Q1 0.8 h/week each; Jun–Aug 6.4 h/week each. Other team-lead duties (coaching, complaint escalations, CAT reserve reviews) unchanged in scope.

catalogue.title: Finance note on paid severity, $2,500–$10,000 band, Q1 vs Jun–Aug
catalogue.text: Average paid amount, $2,500–$10,000 band: Q1 $5,610; Jun–Aug $5,370 (−4.3%). Comment: roof-replacement claims priced from the vendor estimating schedule, which usually settle lower, were 31% of band closures in Jun–Aug against 18% in Q1, because many CAT-0414 claims closed late. No mix-adjusted comparison has been produced yet. Supplementary payments within 60 days of settlement: Q1 3.1%, Jun–Aug 3.4%. Overpayment is not measured outside the Internal Audit re-test.

catalogue.title: Complaints team note on Jun–Aug complaint sources and coding
catalogue.source: Customer complaints team lead, note dated 9 September
catalogue.text: Of 222 formal complaints in Jun–Aug, 64 came from broker telephone calls. Under the pre-April process these would not have been logged. 49 relate to CAT-0414 coverage or depreciation disputes. The logging agent assigns categories from free text, and there is no quality check on coding. Several complaints coded 'Delay' also cite a coverage decision. We cannot produce a like-for-like series against pre-April data.

catalogue.title: Learning and training records, claims unit, Jan–Aug
catalogue.text: Annual fraud-awareness module: 100% of adjusters completed by 30 April. Quillfast viewer training: 6 adjusters attended in March, and a recorded session is available to all. Contract adjuster induction: 3 days, 2–4 June. Team-lead coaching skills workshop: half day, 14 May, all three team leads. No other mandatory training due in the period.

catalogue.title: Post-settlement customer satisfaction survey results, Q1 and Q2
catalogue.text: Post-settlement satisfaction (1–5 scale): Q1 4.1 (n=412); Q2 3.7 (n=455). Share of comments mentioning speed or waiting: Q1 12%; Q2 29%. catalogue.title: Statement from Quillfast account manager on service performance
catalogue.source: Letter from Quillfast account manager to Tallowmere Procurement, 8 September
catalogue.text: We are aware of concerns raised internally at Tallowmere. Apart from the March incident, for which we have issued a service credit, Quillfast has met or beaten every contractual indexing service level every month. We would welcome a workshop with your adjusters to configure viewer shortcuts. A move back to your previous provider would incur early-termination charges under clause 14.2.

hypotheses.text: The 1 April revision of the delegated settlement authority matrix is the main cause of the sustained rise in turnaround. It routes $2,500–$10,000 settlements to three team leads, who cannot keep up with the approvals.
The claim surge from the April CAT-0414 hail event is the main driver of turnaround staying near 18 days through June–August.
The May loss of two senior adjusters reduced adjuster capacity and is the main driver of the turnaround increase.
The March switch to Quillfast document imaging is delaying claim files and is a main driver of the turnaround increase.
The interim $2,500 adjuster authority limit is reducing overpayments on $2,500–$10,000 settlements.

actions.text: With Internal Audit, add interim approval capacity for the $2,500–$10,000 band, for example by certifying experienced senior adjusters as second approvers or temporarily moving other team-lead duties elsewhere. Keep a second review on every claim in the band, and track time pending approval weekly.
Immediately restore adjusters' sole settlement authority to $10,000 to clear the approval tray, without waiting for Internal Audit.
Put the three team leads on performance improvement plans for slow settlement approvals.
Make the $2,500 adjuster limit the permanent authority standard now, and fund a fourth team-lead post dedicated to approvals.

truth.groundTruthNarrative: In February an internal audit found overpayments in mid-value settlements that only one adjuster had reviewed. The agreed interim control cut adjuster settlement authority from $10,000 to $2,500 from 1 April. From then on, every settlement between $2,500 and $10,000 (about 52% of closures) went to one of three team leads for approval. Nobody assessed the workload impact. The team leads now approve about five times as many items as before, work about 6 hours of overtime a week each, and review each file in about 9 minutes. Even so, approvals arrive faster than they can clear them, so the tray has grown to about 455 items. Claims in that band now spend about 16 days waiting for approval, against 0.7 days before. Every other stage is unchanged, and claims under $2,500 and over $10,000 are also unchanged. The tray began growing in the week of 6 April, before the hail event. The VP's explanation (storm volume, lost adjusters, the new imaging vendor) does not hold up. Claim volume and adjuster headcount were back to normal by June. Adjuster investigation time and document intake time did not change. The rise in complaints coincides with the longer turnaround, but a change in how complaints are logged on 1 April muddies the comparison. Whether the new control actually reduces overpayments will not be known until Internal Audit re-tests in December. The right response is to add approval capacity while keeping a second review on every claim in the band, not to remove the control or blame the team leads.

answers.rationale: C5 shows the authority cut took effect on 1 April and moved $2,500–$10,000 settlements to team leads with no workload assessment. C2 shows the whole increase in that band (10.4 to 26.0 days) is in the pending-approval stage (0.7 to 16.0). The bands not affected by the rule did not change, and the overall mean rose from about 9.7 to 18 days as a result. C6 shows the tray began growing in the week of 6 April, before the storm, and kept growing through August. E6 and E4 only hint at this.

The storm came two weeks after the authority change, so the timing is confounded. C6 shows the tray growing from the week of 6 April, before the storm, and inflow in Jun–Aug back at the pre-storm level of about 212 a week while the tray still grew. C2 shows that claims under $2,500, handled by the same adjusters, did not change, and that investigation time did not change. C1 confirms that volume returned to baseline by June.

Turnaround rose in April, before the May departures (E1, E3). Headcount was back to 24 from June, yet turnaround stayed near 18 days. C2 shows the adjuster investigation stage is flat, and C3 shows caseloads and overtime back at Q1 levels.

Turnaround in March, after the cutover, was normal (9.9 days). C2 shows intake/indexing time flat in every band (0.8–1.0 days). C4 shows Quillfast indexes faster than the old provider, with only one outage, cleared in March. Staff complaints are about usability, not delay. The vendor letter (C12) comes from an interested party and is not needed.

No one is measuring overpayments until the Internal Audit re-test in December (C5). The 4% drop in average paid amount in C7 is confounded by a shift toward roof claims and is not mix-adjusted. Supplementary payments barely moved. The evidence cannot tell whether the control is working.

The case for causation rests on four points. Timing: the change took effect on 1 April and the tray started rising in the week of 6 April, before the storm. Mechanism: the change routes the band to three team leads (C5), whose inflow rose from 38 to over 200 items a week (C6). Comparison: only the band covered by the rule changed, while claims under $2,500 and over $10,000 did not (C2). Rival ruled out: volume and staffing returned to normal while the delay persisted.

Claims linked to the storm had essentially stopped arriving by June (C1), and tray inflow was back to the pre-storm level (C6). The sustained delay is entirely in the approval stage of the band covered by the rule, and claims under $2,500 did not change (C2). The storm may have worsened April, but the evidence goes against it explaining June–August.

Complaints and turnaround rose together. However, E5 states that a new complaints module started logging broker phone complaints and created the 'Delay' category on 1 April, the same day the rise began. C8 adds storm coverage disputes and unchecked coding. That leaves a co-occurrence without a like-for-like comparison.
C2 shows adjuster investigation time flat in every band (for example 6.9 to 7.0 days). C3 shows caseloads and overtime back at Q1 levels once the contract backfill arrived (E3).

This tackles the approval shortfall that is now established (C2, C6). It keeps the second review the audit required and involves Internal Audit, so it fits the interim nature of the control described in C5.

C5 records overpayments in 17 of 120 sampled settlements under sole adjuster authority, a High audit finding. Restoring that authority unilaterally would remove a protective control. The same speed gain is available by adding approval capacity instead.

C6 shows the team leads approving about five times their previous volume, at 9 minutes a file and with extra overtime. The delay comes from routing about 200 items a week to three people without any workload assessment (C5), not from poor performance.

This could be right if the December re-test shows the $2,500 limit reduces overpayments enough to justify a permanent post. That benefit is not yet established (H5 is unknown), and C5 says permanent thresholds and resourcing should wait for the re-test.

Together the three reads establish the mechanism, the timing, and a comparison across bands that rules out the volume, staffing and imaging explanations. That is enough to commit to a capacity fix that keeps the control in place (A1). Only the decision about the control's permanent level has to wait.

truth.authoringNotes: Trap design: the authority change (1 Apr) and the hail storm (14–16 Apr) fall two weeks apart, so monthly figures cannot separate them. Only the weekly tray data (C6) and the band split (C2) can. The initial file hints at the real cause only through 'revised DAM live 1 Apr' in E6 and one survey verbatim in E4. The VP's account names three plausible causes, each rebutted by specific evidence. E3 alone already counts against the staffing story (the rise predates the departures, and headcount was restored), while the storm and imaging stories need C2/C6 or C4. The unknown item is H5: whether the control is working cannot be judged until the December re-test, and C7's severity figure is explicitly confounded by claim mix. R3 stays association-only because the complaints logging change is disclosed in E5 itself. A4 is premature rather than acceptable because C5 explicitly defers permanent thresholds and resourcing to the re-test. A2 is harmful because the overpayments the control addresses are documented. Arithmetic checks: the band-weighted means give about 9.7 days for Q1 and about 18.1 for Jun–Aug, matching E1. A tray of 455 cleared at 199 a week is about 2.3 weeks, consistent with 16 days pending approval. Inflow of 212 a week against 199 approvals means the tray keeps growing. Possible reviewer objection: whether the storm made April worse is not scored, because R2 is limited to June–August.
